newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup: Tax reform.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup: Tax reform.

text.p: By Jim Middleton (ABC TV Political Correspondent)
"We said we wouldn't revisit that area: we won't." -- Peter Costello this week rejecting persistent demands for a goods and services tax (GST).

In the GST jeer squad, the treasurer is no Johnny come lately. Back in early 1992, Costello was the only coalition frontbencher to dare to suggest publicly that John Hewson had to sell the politics as well as the economics of a consumption tax.
That was six months before Dr Hewson caved in and modified Fightback! in a final, vain attempt to win the so-called unlosable election.
Given the reign of fear that surrounded the Hewson opposition, Costello's early expression of concern was brave, if not foolhardy.
But it also demonstrates the length and depth of the treasurer's scepticism about not only the political marketing of tax reform, but the idea of a GST itself.

Not so John Howard. He's been a long time GST backer -- steadfast through the Hewson years and toeing the party line ever since. He's never recanted his support for the idea, simply repeating the post-1993 mantra that a GST is out because it's been rejected by the voters.
The prime minister knows he can't break his campaign promise not to increase taxes or introduce new ones this term, but he's careful to leave his options open for a second term.
"What I'm going to take to the next election in this whole area is something that I'll decide closer to the election," Howard declared last week.
Compare that with Costello's adamant and blanket opposition.

The prime minister did warn advocates not to warn that a GST would be Australia's "economic elixir" and that there was still "a lot of entrenched opposition" in the community. However, he also noted that he'd supported Fightback!, that the current tax debate was "good" and that the economy needed "a better taxation system".
Plenty of positives there.

By contrast, his treasurer cannot find one kind word of support for the debate let alone the concept. Privately, Costello is scathing about Victorian Premier -- and old enemy -- Jeff Kennett presenting himself as the tax reform champion.
The treasurer believes Kennett is simply in the headline business and would drop off the moment the going got tough.

As for the welfare groups -- the Australian Council of Social Services (ACOSS) and the Brotherhood of Saint Laurence in particular -- Costello thinks they're the most timorous of fair weather sailors who would scurry for a safe haven at the sign of the slightest ripple on the waters. Either that or they'd only countenance a small GST accompanied by big increases in other taxes.

And in public, the contrast with his prime minister could hardly be sharper. While Howard welcomes the tax debate, the treasurer denies a sea change in support for a consumption tax. Far from a broadening in the base of support for tax reform he argues "the chorus of calls" for a GST is coming from exactly the same people who supported John Hewson when he went down in a screaming heap in 1993.

And he'll back his judgment on that against that of the GST brigade: "I reckon I've stood in a few more RSLs than you have and tried to explain it (the GST) to the punters," he said this week. "The punters when they were asked in an open and fair election said no ... What more can you say?"

Well, a fair bit actually. And it's all there in the results of the government's mid-year review of the budget made public at the very news conference where Costello made those sardonic remarks. It goes this way.

One of Paul Keating's desperate attempts to shore up the crumbling tax base has come back to bite the coalition government on the backside. The increase in the company tax rate from 33 to 36 percent was seen -- hardly surprising -- by corporate accountants as nothing more than an opportunity for a bit of tax planning.
A$1.6 billion more tax planning than the Tax Office predicted, as it's turned out.
Low inflation may be what we all want, but it hits tax receipts too by decreasing the speed with which workers move into higher tax brackets.

All of which has helped blow out the budget bottom line by A$3.0 billion. With unemployment on the way up and consumption on the way down the government is showing little enthusiasm for another whack at the out of work and the welfare recipients who bore the brunt of last year's budget cuts.
Fiddling with the A$4.0 billion in the kitty from Keating's L-A-W tax cuts may get the government out of this year's hole. It's also bound to irritate the voters.

But it will also come to irritate ministers because it's no permanent solution. Irritating because constriction of the tax base will increase the demand for cuts which -- as Labor found -- will be harder and harder to come by.
Tax reform is the real solution. Peter Costello may yet rue the day when he was so adamant about his opposition to a GST. John Howard may well not thank him either.
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
